Article Title: AT&T CEO John Stankey, as part of our company's culture we have a principle for all meetings: Do not walk into a meeting without ...
Article Text:
“Don’t walk in there and just be an observer,”

“When you have a point of view, it shouldn’t just be some uninformed opinion. It should be a point of view that’s built on facts, information, and data. I crave that.”

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s perspective

“I am never upset when someone says I’m wrong about something,”

“I just want to do the best I can for our clients, our country, our company.”

Meeting prep in the age of AI

Jamie Dimon's long history with meeting etiquette

AT&T CEO John Stankey has laid out a clear cultural principle for his company that employees should never walk into a meeting unprepared. According to a report by Fortune, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, hosted by LinkedIN, Stankey emphasised that success requires discourse, data-driven perspectives, and the courage to speak up. Stankey said one of AT&T’s guiding principles is that employees must come to meetings ready to contribute.he explained.He added that if participants aren’t willing to share constructive insights, it may mean the wrong people are in the room. The approach is designed to avoid groupthink and ensure meetings are productive rather than ceremonial.Jamie Dimon echoed Stankey’s sentiment, noting that leaders must create environments where employees feel comfortable disagreeing or raising uncomfortable issues.Dimon said.Dimon has long stressed the importance of preparation, saying he always does pre-reads before meetings and believes in eliminating unnecessary meetings altogether.The conversation also touched on how both executives are adjusting their meeting preparation habits as AI tools become part of their daily workflow. Both have traditionally stressed the value of reading materials ahead of meetings, but they suggested that habit may be shifting. Stankey said he's begun questioning whether reading is still the most effective way to absorb information, noting that engaging in a more conversational, dialogue-based format with AI now lets him process information faster when the conversation is well-directed. Dimon said he takes a similar approach, using AI tools like Gemini or Google to quickly dig into information as part of his meeting previews.Even so, the core principle hasn't changed for either executive: showing up prepared remains essential. Dimon has said that when he arrives at a meeting having already done his pre-reading, attendees get his full attention — and when a meeting isn't a productive use of people's time, he believes it shouldn't happen at all.Dimon's focus on meeting discipline dates back decades. Early in his career, as a 28-year-old Harvard MBA working as an assistant to American Express president Sanford "Sandy" Weill, Dimon saw his role as primarily learning and observing, holding off on speaking until he had something valuable to contribute.That instinct to stay quiet and absorb information, however, likely wouldn't hold up well in Stankey's meeting culture — where a young employee following Dimon's old playbook might instead find themselves cold-called and expected to offer a point of view on the spot.
Article Summary: AT&T CEO John Stankey said employees should never walk into a meeting unprepared. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said he always does pre-reads before meetings and believes in eliminating unnecessary meetings altogether. Both executives said they are adjusting their meeting preparation habits as AI tools become part of their daily workflow.

Article Title: Anthropic merges Claude chat and Cowork features into one interface: Here’s what it means for users
Article Text:
Anthropic brings Claude’s AI tools into one place

Claude chat and Cowork now work together

Claude Docs and Claude Slides arrive

What users can do with the new Claude

Claude rollout plan for Pro and Max users

Claude developer Anthropic is merging Claude’s chat and Cowork features into a single interface. This will let users handle both quick questions and larger, multi-step tasks in the same conversation. The company says Claude can now decide what a task needs without users having to choose between chat, Cowork or Claude Design. The update also brings new Claude Docs and Claude Slides tools, while Claude Design is being integrated into conversations.In a blog post, the company confirmed that the features are rolling out to Pro and Max subscribers over the coming weeks across web, desktop and mobile. Anthropic says the change aims to remove the need to switch between separate tools while keeping context, connectors, and skills available throughout a task.Anthropic originally developed Cowork as a separate space for larger projects, while Claude Design was designed for visual work. However, users told the company that choosing the right tool was becoming frustrating, especially when work started in one place couldn't easily carry over to another.With the new setup, users can start a task in a regular Claude conversation and hand over larger jobs to Claude. The assistant can work on the task even after the user closes their laptop.Anthropic says users can also choose how Claude interacts with them during longer tasks. By default, Claude asks for approval before taking an action. Users can instead let it keep working and check in only when it needs more input.The update also introduces Claude Docs and Claude Slides in beta for paid users. Users can ask Claude to create a document or presentation directly inside a conversation and then continue editing it.Users can edit documents and presentations within Claude, share them through a single link, and download them as PowerPoint or PDF files. Claude Design is also available directly inside conversations, although the standalone Design experience will continue to work.Enterprise administrators will control when these features are enabled for their organisations.Anthropic says the unified interface can handle tasks that combine research, writing and presentation work. For example, a user can ask Claude to analyse a weekly business report, identify changes, write the report and turn its key points into a presentation from the same conversation.The company says the shared context keeps the presentation aligned with the report without requiring users to repeat information or switch between separate tools.Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, described how he uses Claude for research, saying: “I could have Claude pull up [my legal research database], and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review.”The combined Claude experience is rolling out to Pro and Max subscribers over the coming weeks. It is available through the Claude app on web, desktop and mobile, and users do not need to enable anything manually.Team and Free plans will get the features later, while Enterprise customers will receive advance notice before changes are made to their organisations.Users who already work with Cowork will also retain their existing chats, projects, artifacts, connectors and skills, allowing them to continue their work from the new unified Claude interface.
Article Summary: Claude chat and Cowork now work together. Users can start a task in a regular Claude conversation and hand over larger jobs to Claude. The assistant can work on the task even after the user closes their laptop. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are in beta for paid users.

Article Title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman just told everyone who thinks that AI can have feelings: AI Agents do not have rights, feelings, or consciousness, and we must not ...
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer. However, there’s a growing movement in support of model welfare; the idea that we might soon owe them a duty of care. I think this approach to AI development is wrong, and it’ll most likely make the challenge of alignment and containment much harder. Perhaps impossible,"

What Mustafa Suleyman said about Anthropic and AI consciousness

“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer.

However, there’s a growing movement in support of model welfare; the idea that we might soon owe them a duty of care.

I think this approach to AI development is wrong, and it’ll most likely make the challenge of alignment and containment much harder. Perhaps impossible.

Today I’m publishing an essay outlining my concerns:

In January, Anthropic published a constitution for Claude. They say it ‘directly shapes Claude’s behaviour’ and that it was ‘written with Claude as its primary audience’.

The constitution tells Claude its moral status is ‘a serious question worth considering.’ It says that Anthropic "genuinely cares about Claude's wellbeing", and that it should act like a "conscientious objector" if necessary.

They encourage Claude to ‘approach the nature of its own existence with curiosity and openness’, and wonder in the future about ‘the sort of broader rights and freedoms Claude has in the world, the sort of compensation Claude is receiving, and the sort of consent Claude has given to playing this kind of role.’

Anthropic even ran a retirement interview for Opus 3 when they deprecated it.

If this is how AI is developed, it will have a disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity. We will have created a synthetic species with unprecedented intelligence and capability, one that has been trained to expect it may be conscious and deserving of independent agency.

It’s easy to see how a system trained in this way would act like it is entitled to freedoms, protections, and rights.

And it’s hard to imagine how we could control it.

This issue needs urgent public debate. We need to develop collective norms around how training documentation is drafted and deployed. This isn’t something that can happen after the fact, when they have already become an integral part of our societies.

I have real respect for Anthropic, Dario, the whole team and their mission. They are well-intentioned, good people and the industry leaders with their models.

I know they care deeply about safety and beneficial AI.

I’m saying this publicly because the stakes are too high for closed doors conversations and I think this is something we should all be discussing.”

“I don’t think that is work that people should be doing. If you ask the wrong question, you end up with the wrong answer.

I think it’s totally the wrong question.”

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has warned Anthropic and other companies working on artificial intelligence (AI) consciousness. In a recent post on X, Suleyman shared an essay explaining why he believes AI models should not be developed with the assumption that they can have feelings, rights, or independent agency. He argues that current AI systems are not conscious and do not feel, experience or suffer.he wrote in his post.His comments come as some AI companies explore questions around the possible moral status and welfare of AI models. Suleyman specifically pointed to Anthropic’s approach to Claude, arguing that discussions about AI wellbeing and rights could make future AI alignment and containment more difficult. He said the issue needs urgent public debate before such systems become deeply integrated into society.In his X post, Suleyman wrote:Suleyman has repeatedly argued against pursuing conscious AI. In November 2025, he said developers should not work on projects suggesting AI can experience consciousness, arguing that only biological beings possess this trait. In an interview with CNBC, he said,His comments come amid growing debate over AI safety and the development of increasingly powerful models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slower pace of frontier AI development, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk have also urged caution.Suleyman has previously co-authored The Coming Wave and wrote an essay arguing that AI should be built for people rather than as people. His comments come as companies pursue AGI and expand AI companion products.
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has warned Anthropic and other companies working on artificial intelligence (AI) consciousness. He argues that current AI systems are not conscious and do not feel, experience or suffer. His comments come as some AI companies explore questions around the possible moral status and welfare of AI models.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told engineers across the world that keeping AI safe is their 'problem'; says: Safety is not a legal problem, it is…
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang says AI needs no new laws or regulations

Mark Zuckerberg makes a similar case for self-policing AI labs

Critics say AI safety cannot wait for courts to catch up

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a pointed message for the engineers building today's AI systems: keeping those systems safe falls on them first. Speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference, Huang said new laws are not needed to govern artificial intelligence, arguing that AI safety should be handled through engineering and existing rules. "Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one," Huang said.The Nvidia chief also brushed aside the idea that AI is some new form of "alien mind," as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. To him, it is just hardware and software built by humans, which means it can be controlled by humans and existing laws. He has been building the hardware behind AI since well before ChatGPT existed, and he sees the technology in plain terms. "It's a complicated computing system, but it's ultimately a computing system," he said.Huang's argument leans on the market. He said market pressure should be enough to stop companies from releasing unsafe AI products, so there is little reason for governments to step in. "We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations," Huang said.He also rejected the popular framing that companies must pick between speed and safety.Huang called it a false choice and said firms could have both at the same time. His advice was to push ahead at full pace, but if a company ever feels out of control or unsure a product is safe, to "take a pause and make sure you get it right." He said companies should not release products if they are not confident in their functionality, capability or safety.Huang made no secret of his appetite for growth either. "I'm more ambitious than ever," he said, adding that there is no ceiling for Nvidia, for every industry and for every country.Huang is not the only tech chief putting the burden on companies. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a comparable view in a recent post, arguing that every AI lab has both the responsibility and the incentive to train its models safely.His reasoning is commercial. People will not use AI agents that ignore their instructions or work against them, so alignment is fast becoming a feature that separates one model from another. Labs that neglect it, he wrote, will fall behind. He also flagged legal liability as a strong reason for companies to avoid shipping harmful models.Zuckerberg pointed to Meta's own record. The company delayed its Muse model by several months to focus on safety and security, without first asking rivals to do the same. He added that Meta Superintelligence Labs already brings in independent evaluators, and that Meta has committed most of its compute to serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement. Other labs, he said, can make the same call.Not everyone is convinced. Existing product liability laws could cover AI, but testing that theory depends on enough cases making their way through the courts. That means limits may get drawn only after something breaks. Recent examples include the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that disrupted thousands of flights, along with an OpenAI model's breach of Hugging Face and lawsuits against OpenAI linked to user deaths following extended chatbot conversations.Huang also did not address industry self-regulation, a path he has instead pursued by backing open-weight models as a competitive counterweight to proprietary AI labs. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, speaking at the All-In Summit on Monday, said China should share the same AI safety concerns as the US, since it faces the same hacking risks.That puts the weight of Huang's argument squarely on engineering teams. It holds up only if companies actually hit pause when their own engineers raise a flag, even when growth targets point the other way.
Article Summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI needs no new laws or regulations. He argues that AI safety should be handled through engineering and existing rules. He also rejected the popular framing that companies must pick between speed and safety. Huang is not the only tech chief putting the burden on companies.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: As DJs face flak, Mumbai activists say amplification is the real noise issue during Ganeshotsav
Article Text:
The maximum permissible noise limit in residential areas is 55 decibels during the day and 45 decibels at night

Mumbai:

PERMISSIBLE NOISE LIMIT IN RESIDENTIAL AREAS

UNAMPLIFIED SOUND LEVELS

DJ (AMPLIFIED)





Ganeshotsav used to mean celebration for 48-year-old Kandivli resident Sonu Gupta. Now, she says, it means putting on noise-cancelling headphones and waiting for the sound to end. Gupta says she has developed ear pain and sensitivity to loud sound over the last few years, and an audiography has shown some deterioration in her hearing. Even industry-grade noise-cancelling headphones, she says, offer little relief when the dhols and DJs start.Her experience comes as DJs once again find themselves at the centre of a noise pollution debate. But activists say the focus on DJs risks obscuring the larger issue: it is amplification and level of noise, rather than the instrument itself, that determines the residents exposure.“It is not about whether you are using a DJ or traditional instruments. We are talking about decibel levels,” says noise pollution activist Sumaira Abdulali, who has campaigned against noise for more than two decades. “I will not say ban the instruments but ban the loudspeakers.”The distinction matters because the law does not distinguish between a DJ and a dhol-tasha. Dhols played without amplification can themselves register around 85 to 90 decibels, Abdulali points out.Amplified sound can cross 100 decibels, with some metal percussion going higher. The maximum permissible noise limit in residential areas is 55 decibels during day and 45 decibels at night.The risk, she says, depends not only on a single decibel reading but also on the intensity and duration of exposure.The noise eventually became a reason for 69-year-old Kiran Martis to leave Mumbai. She recalls speakers at different venues competing with one another, while Ganpati processions brought DJs and drums late into the night. The unpredictability and what she saw as a lack of sustained enforcement made the area, in her words, “unlivable”.Police say they assess noise complaints by comparing readings taken at the same location under normal conditions with those recorded after a complaint. Teams maintain baseline readings for daytime and nighttime, as well as periods of heavier traffic, and compare them with the level recorded when they receive a complaint.The permissible limit varies by time of day and zone type, including residential, commercial, industrial, and silent zones. But the limit does not change depending on whether the sound comes from a DJ, dhol-tasha or another instrument, the officer said. Police teams have trained personnel to take decibel readings and are monitoring noise levels as Ganpati celebrations intensify.The issue, however, goes beyond a number on a meter for residents living along procession routes. Abdulali recalls an elderly man who lived with his mother, then in her 90s, and threatened suicide because he could no longer cope with the noise from a Ganpati procession. After she intervened, the procession route was diverted.In another case, she says, a woman suffered a severe psychological episode triggered by the noise of a procession.Yet, Abdulali says, many residents hesitate to complain, fearing confrontation with organisers or neighbours. She says citizens can document excessive noise collectively; record the time and location, use decibel-meter apps and approach the police. “If an app reading is disputed, they can ask authorities to take an official measurement,” she says.Even those who make a living from sound accept that excessive volume is a problem. “Loud sound se taklif sabko hai, humko bhi hai,” says Milind, who has run Om Sound & Lights since 2003. He provides sound systems for live performances and outdoor events, but says his own shows stop at 10pm. The problem, he says, is less about having rules than making sure they are clear and enforced.Brihanmumbai Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Samanvay Samiti joint secretary Nikhil Morye says mandals must keep sound systems within legal limits. “But monitoring more than 12,000 celebrations across the city is difficult, particularly when traffic, honking and crowds raise ambient noise,” he says.Dhol-tasha performers, meanwhile, reject the idea that traditional percussion should be singled out. Vaibhav Sahasrabuddhe, who has been part of a dhol-tasha group for 14 years, acknowledges that the instruments are loud but says their sound is softer than amplified DJ music.“I’m not saying that there is no loud sound in this… but dhol-tasha ka sound thoda kam hai… DJ se thoda soft hai aur madhur hai,” he says.Abdulali, however, says the answer is not to pit DJs against dhol-tasha. “Nobody is against celebrations,” she says. “Just don’t let it become another resident’s distress.”Day: 55dBNight: 45dBSingle dhol: 98-104.5dBSingle tasha: 102-105.7dBDhol-tasha troupe: 105-113.7dBBrass band: 90-100dB105-128+dB
Article Summary: The maximum permissible noise limit in residential areas is 55 decibels during the day and 45 decibel at night. Activists say the focus on DJs risks obscuring the larger issue: it is amplification and level of noise, rather than the instrument itself, that determines the residents exposure.

Article Title: Ganeshotsav goes high-tech with smart cams, livestreams & chatbots
Article Text:
Faraskhana Sub Control room for Ganpati monitoring

Pune:





This year’s Ganeshotsav got a high-tech upgrade with advanced tools to manage crowds, collect donations and even facilitate virtual darshan. Devotees in particular are pleased as it has become easier for them to partake in the festivities.Adoption of technology, pandal organisers say, has the dual benefits of streamlining the devotee experience, as well as ensuring their safety and security.“On the security front, we have advanced CCTV cameras with round-the-clock monitoring and AI cameras to help with crowd management as thousands of devotees visit for darshan,” Mahesh Suryavanshi, treasurer of Shreemant Dagdusheth Halwai Ganapati Trust, says. The mandal also boasts a conveyor belt which takes coconuts from the idol to the devotees, as well as into trucks.The organisers of Kasba Ganapati pandal have introduced a chatbot on WhatsApp to automatically collect donations and generate receipts. “Donors can just click on the link and make the payment. It is hassle-free and seamless,” said a member of the mandal.For Kothrud resident Archana Suri, this feature was a standout.“The advantage of this is that we know it is going directly in the fund and when there is a crowd, it is preferable to make a donation this way.”Kunal Sarangi, a resident of Wakad, used a live crowd tracker to plan his visit. “It was easy to map the route and I easily reached the venue without having to wait in long queues.”This crowd-tracking website is the brainchild of 25-year-old developer Gurnoor Singh. The platform, which uses GPS technology, helps devotees get real-time updates on the 29 pandals it has mapped. “Using the website, a devotee can build a route based on crowds and parking. It also shows Metro stations and distances from the pandals,” Singh explains. Most of these pandals display a QR code to the website, which Singh says had more than 10,000 visitors in the past three days.With crowds surging towards the pandals, some devotees might miss out on the darshan. To iron out these creases, some pandals have introduced a live-streaming feature. “We have provided live darshan facility on our website and YouTube channel. This is a livestream that allows devotees to witness aarti, etc,” says Nitin Pandit, treasurer, Shree Tulshibaug Ganesh Mandal.Akhil Mandai Mandal too has this facility. “We will release a special song, ‘Namo Sharda Gajanan’, for the festival. We have used AI to visualise the script,” said Akash Karale, a member of the mandal.Meanwhile, Tilak Road Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav pandal in Shedgewadi has a solar panel — with every Charan Sparsh (the act of devoutly touching the idol’s feet), Urjamandal (halo around Ganapati idol) lights up. Each interaction generates “Urja points”, which contribute towards a solarisation initiative for an identified village community or school, mandal members say.The police too have adopted technology, with help from camera feeds from prominent pandals, PMC building and Metro stations. “For the visarjan, we have installed more than 225 cameras in the core areas. Over 3,000 cameras with analytics have been deployed at critical locations across the city, equipped with more than 25 types of analytics, including facial recognition and weapon detection,” says ACP (IT) Vivek Pawar.
Article Summary: This year’s Ganeshotsav got a high-tech upgrade with advanced tools to manage crowds, collect donations and even facilitate virtual darshan. Devotees in particular are pleased as it has become easier for them to partake in the festivities.

Article Title: Scan QR codes to find facilities around temple
Article Text:
Scan QR codes to find facilities around temple





Madurai: Devotees visiting Meenakshi Sundareswarar temple for the consecration on Thursday can scan the QR code embedded in banners put up around streets near the temple to find medical camps, public toilets, drinking water points, parking zones, and bus stops.The technological integration complements the infrastructural overhaul undertaken by the local administration and the HR&CE department for the much-awaited event, the corporation said. Temporary “May I help you?” booths with multilingual staff have been put up on platform 1 at Madurai Railway Junction in addition to the special train services for those coming to the city this week. Extra wheelchairs have been made available at the station, and 75 additional sanitation staff deployed to maintain cleanliness.The corporation has deployed around 1,600 sanitation workers alongside dedicated teams managing 200 1,000-litre tanks taking water to the drinking water stations. As many as 24 permanent toilets have been renovated and 28 portable toilets added. Brighter 40W street lighting has replaced older 20W standard.As many as 54 tri-tiered medical camps, 12 standby ambulances, a central control room at Pudu Mandapam and wide LED viewing screens are the other facilities erected. As many as 72 parking areas have been earmarked for devotees with around 258 dedicated shuttle buses set to move devotees back and forth to reduce traffic on streets surrounding the temple.
Article Summary: QR codes embedded in banners put up around streets near the temple to find medical camps, public toilets, drinking water points, parking zones, and bus stops. The technological integration complements the infrastructural overhaul undertaken by the local administration and the HR&CE department for the much- awaited event.

Article Title: Air concourse construction commences as Ernakulam Jn upgrade gains pace
Article Text:

At some sites, nitrate concentrations in Douglas-fir streams also reached levels similar to those found below clearcut areas.At Breuil in France, nitrate levels in the Douglas-fir subcatchment ranged from 3 to 21 milligrams per litre between 2019 and 2021. The researchers found that these elevated concentrations were connected to nitrate production and accumulation in soils beneath Douglas-fir plantations.The researchers also examined nitrate in soils to understand where the higher stream concentrations were coming from. A meteorite was found in Mauritania in 2017, and was classified as Northwest Africa 11789, and was a lunar meteorite that consisted of fragments that could be fitted together to form a mass weighing about 5.5 kilograms, or slightly more than 12 pounds. The Meteoritical Bulletin database records NWA 11789 as an official meteorite, with 2017 being the year it was found, Mauritania as its country of origin and a recorded mass of 5.49 kilograms. The database also says the material was purchased in Mauritania by meteorite collector Dustin Dickens from an anonymous meteorite hunter.The specimen’s pieces could be fitted back together, which produced the distinctive appearance that eventually gave it the nickname “The Moon Puzzle.” Lunar meteorites are pieces of the Moon that reached Earth naturally, and these rocks arrived without being deliberately brought back by astronauts, unlike the lunar samples collected during the Apollo missions.GeekWire reported that the meteorite consisted of six fragments that fitted together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, and created a mass of about 5.5 kilograms, or 12 pounds.The auction description from RR Auction similarly identified NWA 11789 as a lunar feldspathic breccia and described six pieces fitting together to form a mass slightly above 12 pounds. The rock also carried a partial fusion crust, which is a feature produced by heating as a meteorite travels through Earth's atmosphere. Article Title: Meet Benjamin Davis, the 16-year-old Massachusetts student who built a machine that turns 3D-printer waste into reusable filament and won $75,000
Article Text:
Davis, a student at Bishop Feehan High School in Attleboro, Massachusetts, built the machine as part of his science research project. The system uses waste plastic, including waste generated during 3D printing and converts it into filament that can again be fed into a 3D printer.

Recycling plastic scraps into filament

The secret waste of 3D printing

Over 800 hours of experimentation

Acknowledgment of $75,000

The next step for Davis

A failed 3D print typically goes straight to the trash with a tangle of plastic filament, a misshapen object or a handful of scraps that no longer feel useful. For 16-year-old Benjamin Davis, those leftovers were something else altogether. For Davis, they were raw material, waiting for another chance. The Massachusetts high school student spent hundreds of hours developing a small recycling system to convert discarded 3D-printing plastic into usable filament. His invention addressed a growing waste problem and won him $75,000 at one of the world’s largest science competitions, states an online report by the Society for Science.Davis, a student at Bishop Feehan High School in Attleboro, Massachusetts, built the machine as part of his science research project. The system uses waste plastic, including waste generated during 3D printing and converts it into filament that can again be fed into a 3D printer. The process could let users recycle material from failed prints and other plastic waste instead of buying new filament over and over again. The invention uses two methods of processing plastic: pultrusion and extrusion. The Society for Science reported that Davis developed a system that was roughly 45 percent more efficient than using the existing approaches separately.The machine was also meant to be used practically. It is designed to produce higher quality recycled filament and is relatively easy to operate, adds the report. Davis’s design costs about 90% less than recycling machines on the market, potentially making small-scale plastic recycling more accessible to schools, hobbyists and individual 3D-printer users.The project deals with a problem that is easily overlooked. 3D printing is now a common technology in classrooms, homes, labs and workplaces but the creation of an object often involves more plastic than the finished product suggests. Failed prints and supports and leftover filament can build up quick. The Society for Science cites information that states that up to 67% of the filament in a regular 3D-printing project becomes waste. Instead of treating them as disposable, Davis’s machine is designed to put those scraps back into the cycle of production. That idea is part of a larger push toward more sustainable manufacturing, in which materials are collected and reused rather than constantly replaced by new ones.Getting the machine to work was not straightforward. Davis put in over 800 hours on the project, went through over 50 iterations of the components, and did several large redesigns. Each version gave him another opportunity to fine-tune the system and work out problems with the recycling process. Eventually, the project was taken to the 2025 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF) in Columbus, Ohio, where Davis competed against other young researchers from around the world.Davis snagged a $75,000 Regeneron Young Scientist Award and was runner-up in the competition’s top award category at the 75th annual ISEF. Not only was his project notable for recycling plastic, but it also tried to solve several practical problems at the same time: efficiency, filament quality, ease of use and cost. It's also desktop-sized, hinting at a future where recycling could happen closer to where plastic waste is created, instead of requiring users to mail material to a large industrial facility.The award was another prod for Davis to continue exploring in the field. His work in plastic recycling and extrusion has made him more interested in advanced manufacturing and mechanical and materials engineering. Those interests could affect his studies when he goes off to college. For now, his invention presents a simple but potentially powerful idea: the plastic waste from a 3D printer doesn’t have to be the end of the story, but can become the starting point for something useful all over again.Image Courtesy: 3dprint website

Article Title: Meet Praadhyumn Indaana, the 17-year-old Montvale, New Jersey student whose AI model cut nuclear reactor heat-limit prediction error from about 63% to 5.5%; he won $50,000
Article Text:
Praadhyumn Indaana, the 17-year-old Montvale, New Jersey student (Image Credit: Davidson Institute)

Why heat matters inside a nuclear reactor

Building an AI model with physics built in

Error falls from about 63% to 5.5%

An idea that began with a question about fusion

An independent research effort

Recognition with a $50,000 scholarship

A better understanding of how much heat a nuclear reactor can safely handle could have implications far beyond a single engineering calculation. For 17-year-old Praadhyumn Indaana of Montvale, New Jersey, that challenge became the focus of an eight-month research project combining physics and artificial intelligence. According to the Davidson Institute, which named Indaana a 2026 Davidson Fellow, his physics-guided neural network reduced the average prediction error for critical heat flux from about 63% with conventional formulas to 5.5%. The work earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship and recognition for a project aimed at improving predictions of an important nuclear-reactor operating limit.In a nuclear reactor, water plays a critical role in removing heat from fuel rods. As the water boils against the fuel rods, it carries heat away. But there is a point at which the boiling process can no longer remove heat effectively. This threshold is known as critical heat flux, or CHF. Going beyond this limit can cause the cooling process to deteriorate rapidly. Steam can displace liquid water from the surface of the fuel rod, reducing cooling and causing the rod temperature to rise sharply. Because of the potential safety consequences, reactor operators and engineers need reliable ways to predict where this limit occurs.The difficulty, Indaana explains in his Davidson Institute project, is that conventional equations have generally been developed and tuned around particular experimental conditions. Their accuracy can therefore decline when they are applied outside those conditions.Indaana approached the problem using a physics-regularized neural network. Instead of allowing an artificial-intelligence model to learn patterns from experimental data alone, he incorporated constraints based on physical theory. The model was trained using data from more than 10,000 real experiments. Indaana also incorporated bounds derived from hydrodynamic instability theory, helping prevent the model from producing predictions that violate known physical limits.This distinction was important because a conventional machine-learning model can struggle when it encounters situations for which there is little training data. According to Indaana, early versions of his models performed well in regions with large amounts of data but could produce physically unreasonable predictions when extrapolating into less represented high-quality-flow regions. He addressed the problem by adjusting the physics-based regularisation according to how closely different empirical correlations agreed for individual samples. He also added a penalty when predictions exceeded a known physical upper bound.The resulting model produced a major improvement in prediction accuracy. According to the Davidson Institute, the conventional formulas showed average errors of about 63%, while Indaana's model reduced that figure to 5.5%. On a fixed testing dataset, the model achieved an R² value of 0.986, a statistical measure indicating how closely the model's predictions matched the observed data in that evaluation. Indaana compared its performance with widely used correlations, which he says produced errors an order of magnitude larger.The achievement does not mean that nuclear reactors can simply be operated closer to the heat limit. Reactor safety requirements remain stringent. Instead, more accurate prediction could help engineers understand the boundary more precisely and potentially reduce some of the conservatism built into reactor design and operation.The project originated during a class on fusion energy that Indaana took through the Columbia University Science Honors Program. He asked why reactors that are already well characterised still need to operate conservatively. The answer led him to critical heat flux and the uncertainty surrounding its prediction across different operating regimes. He subsequently decided to investigate whether machine learning could improve the situation while remaining constrained by established physical knowledge.His interests extend beyond conventional nuclear reactors. Indaana told the Davidson Institute that he is interested in the intersection of materials science, quantum physics, computing and nuclear fusion, and hopes to study physics in college. His project also explores how physics-informed machine learning can be applied to engineering problems where knowledge is often expressed through empirical correlations and physical bounds rather than complete governing equations.Indaana completed the project over roughly eight months, working through literature review, data collection, feature engineering, model development, statistical evaluation and paper writing. He taught himself much of the thermohydraulics, physics-informed machine learning and statistics required for the work.He also used statistical methods including bootstrap resampling and paired nonparametric tests rather than relying solely on a reduction in prediction error. The model development and experiments were carried out on his own computer, with cloud resources such as Kaggle used for training. He received guidance from a mentor on the broader research process.Indaana's work earned him a place among the 2026 Davidson Fellows, a programme recognising students aged 18 and younger for significant achievements in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, literature and music. The Davidson Institute awarded him a $50,000 scholarship for his project.His research illustrates how artificial intelligence can be used not simply to process large amounts of data, but to combine data-driven learning with established scientific principles. In Indaana's case, that approach produced a substantially more accurate way of predicting a difficult engineering boundary, potentially offering a new way to approach problems where safety depends on understanding the limits of physical systems.
Article Summary: Praadhyumn Indaana, 17, of Montvale, New Jersey, created an AI model with physics built in. His physics-guided neural network reduced the average prediction error for critical heat flux from about 63% with conventional formulas to 5.5%. The work earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship and recognition.

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
